For every block of 11 consecutive integers
\[
\{a+1,a+2,\dots,a+11\},
\]
the following edges form an 11-cycle using differences \(4\) or \(7\):
\[
a+1,a+5,a+9,a+2,a+6,a+10,a+3,a+7,a+11,a+4,a+8,a+1.
\]
Thus an independent set can contain at most \(5\) elements from any 11 consecutive integers.

Partition \(\{1,\dots,1980\}\) into \(180\) blocks of length \(11\). Each contributes at most \(5\), so at most \(900\) elements from \(\{1,\dots,1980\}\). The remaining \(9\) numbers \(1981,\dots,1989\) contain the four disjoint pairs
\[
(1981,1985),(1982,1986),(1983,1987),(1984,1988),
\]
so at most \(4\) elements from these pairs plus possibly \(1989\), hence at most \(5\). Therefore
\[
|S|\le 900+5=905.
\]

For the lower bound, take all numbers congruent modulo \(11\) to one of
\[
\{1,3,4,6,9\}.
\]
No two of these residues differ by \(4\) or \(7\) modulo \(11\), so this set has no two elements differing by exactly \(4\) or \(7\). Since
\[
1989=180\cdot 11+9,
\]
the residues \(1,\dots,9\) each occur \(181\) times, so the construction has size
\[
5\cdot 181=905.
\]

Thus the largest possible number of elements is
\[
\boxed{905}.
\]
